style: Read as a calm, confident product narrator for a short demo film. Unhurried, warm, clear. Light emphasis on the product names ClickHouse, Trigger.dev, Valhalla, and on the payoff at the end. Natural pauses between sentences.

beats.text: Where should you open a coffee shop in Amsterdam? Watch the answer draw itself.
No wall of text. A Trigger dot dev agent calls ClickHouse, tool by tool, and each result paints itself onto the map — rivals, opportunity, three top sites, a real walk catchment.

The winner is Nieuw-West — a dense residential edge with just one café anywhere nearby. The name comes from real boundary geometry. The numbers are the ones the score ranked on. And the thirteen-thousand-person walk reach? Measured by Valhalla against the actual street network. Not guessed.
You don't read the answer — you argue with it. Ask for walkability; the map re-scores live.
And it scales. Food and drink across Amsterdam — thousands of points, too big for the chat stream's one-megabyte cap. So it never touches it: it lands in ClickHouse, read straight from the browser.
Save a site — change data capture streams it into ClickHouse, against seventy-five million live points.
One last thing — no web server. The whole app is a row in ClickHouse. Every file, a row.
The agent runs on Trigger dot dev's cloud. Ask a question, get a live map — not a wall of text. Millions of points, drawn, not written. That's WhereHouse.
